title: Hardware Security Module
summary: A hardware security module is a tamper-resistant device that generates, stores and uses cryptographic keys inside a boundary the host operating system cannot read across. Keys are created on the module, never leave it in plaintext, and are used through a constrained API that performs signing, decryption, key wrapping or random generation on behalf of an authorised caller. Because the key material exists only inside protected hardware, stealing the key requires physical or logical access to the module rather than a copy of a configuration file, and many modules zeroise their key store in response to detected tampering. HSMs underpin certificate authority private keys, payment key management, code signing, database transparent encryption, disk encryption key hierarchies and cloud KMS backends that offer dedicated or single-tenant hardware. The operational model introduces its own failure modes: poorly controlled administrator roles and quorum settings, weak or shared operator credentials that permit key export, misconfigured network exposure of the module's management interface, backup and restore procedures that either lose the key forever or replicate it into weaker storage, weak entropy on the first initialisation, and audit logging that is disabled or never reviewed. Availability also matters, since an HSM cluster that cannot fail over can take critical signing or payment flows offline, so redundancy and documented recovery are part of the security design rather than an afterthought.
objectives: Describe how an HSM protects key material through tamper resistance, restricted APIs and controlled key export.
Separate operator, administrator and auditor roles and explain why split knowledge and quorum controls matter.
Evaluate an HSM deployment for network exposure, entropy source, backup strategy and firmware currency.
Design high-availability key services so that hardware failure or cluster loss does not break signing or payment flows.
Review HSM audit logs to confirm key usage matches the applications and cryptoperiods that are expected.
Compare dedicated hardware modules, cloud KMS backends and software key stores for a specific key's risk profile.
